item.title: When Grief Goes to the Movies
item.description:
Grief

When Grief Goes to the Movies

Exploring fear and the longing to feel alive through "Fall" and "Fall 2: Deadpoint."

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Cinematherapy uses the personal resonance of films to help clients explore their inner worlds.
  • We can at once want to escape what we feel and reckon with it.
  • By sparking feelings and bodily responses in a safe place, a movie can make painful emotions more accessible.

Sometimes it's easier to connect with our feelings while watching someone else’s story unfold—in the dark among a crowd of strangers. Enter cinematherapy, an adjunct to psychotherapy that uses the personal resonance of films to help clients explore their inner worlds. One framework describes the process in four stages: identification with a character, catharsis, insight into oneself, and universalization—the recognition that we are not alone in our experiences. Research on cinematherapy is in its early days, but the approach offers a novel way to explore difficult feelings.

Take "Fall," the 2022 survival thriller. Becky has withdrawn from life following her husband Dan’s death in a climbing accident. Her friend proposes climbing an abandoned, 2,000-foot television tower to scatter his ashes and help her move forward.

Similarly, "Fall 2: Deadpoint" begins with another loss and another climb. Jax and Luce, who have lost a sister and a friend, respectively, undertake a dangerous plank walk on Thailand’s Mount Kwan to fulfill their deceased loved one’s dream. A rockslide leaves them stranded on a fragile plank thousands of feet above the ground. They have come for closure—but now their lives depend on finding a way back.

Yet why risk death to honor someone who has died?

The answer may lie in seeking reclamation after loss. For Becky, climbing is central to her identity. It is something she shared with Dan—and the activity during which he died. The climb means reclaiming a part of herself that has been dormant since losing him. Jax believes that fulfilling her sister’s dream of tackling Mount Kwan will help resolve her grief while giving her the courage to face the fear of heights her sister had encouraged her to overcome.

But these tribute climbs—an abandoned tower and an exposed mountain walkway—quickly turn into battles to stay alive.

Escaping Grief or Working Through Grief?

In both films, the internal experience of grief is externalized through a climb toward the sky, where paying tribute to a loved one means tempting fate with one’s own life. “You have to do something that makes you feel alive,” Becky says in "Fall"’s closing voiceover, echoing her friend. But are the rush and danger of climbing a viable way to wake up from grief?

At extreme heights, our brains and bodies are doing a lot of work. Information from our eyes, inner ears, and body must be continually integrated to keep us balanced. The vestibular nuclei in the brainstem and the cerebellum help us maintain posture and orient ourselves in space. At the same time, a network that includes the amygdala, anterior insula, and anterior cingulate cortex helps process threat and bodily arousal. With fewer nearby visual reference points, visual information becomes less reliable, which can make it harder to balance and maintain posture. For the characters, these challenges force attention on the immediate challenge of staying alive, leaving little space—at least in the here and now—for grief.

As viewers, we get a dose of that intensity of being up high from the comfort of our seats. We yell at the characters, grip the armrest, hold our breath, and brace for a fall with them. Brain-imaging research on people watching horror movies helps explain why: sudden scares heighten activity in the brain’s threat-response network, while sustained suspense elevates activity in regions that process sights and sounds. The sympathetic nervous system may accelerate our heart rate and breathing, giving us clammy palms. We know we are safe, yet our bodies prepare to respond.

Just as "Fall" and "Fall 2: Deadpoint" offer the experience of wrestling with grief through physical extremes, they also offer the possibility of moving beyond it. Becky’s return to climbing and Jax’s decision to face her fear of heights in her sister’s name illustrate how we can at once want to escape what we feel and reckon with it. We as viewers experience some of the adrenaline and danger while identifying with the longing beneath it: to feel connected to someone we have lost, and to carry them with us in some way as we move forward.

Cinematherapy is based on the idea that films have the power to engage and activate us emotionally. By sparking feelings and bodily responses in a place of safety, a movie can make painful emotions more accessible. For someone who has felt overcome by grief, the rush of watching "Fall" and "Fall 2: Deadpoint" might temporarily restore a feeling of aliveness through witnessing extreme danger. The experience can offer catharsis and, in turn, invite personal reflection: In what ways do we identify with these characters—and what might returning to life after loss look like for us?

item.title: 4 Guilt Trips Adult Children Use When You Say No
item.description:
Parenting

4 Guilt Trips Adult Children Use When You Say No

What to say back to an adult child who tries to bend your "No" into "Yes."

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Saying no to an adult child can bring up guilt, anxiety, and self-doubt.
  • Guilt-inducing reactions can pressure parents to abandon healthy boundaries.
  • Calm, firm, loving responses help parents stay supportive without rescuing.

"No"—it's just a two-letter word, right? Yet, each week, parents who see me for parent coaching sessions lament how the word "no" is loaded with guilt and pain as they see their adult children struggle. Let's be clear: I'm very much OK with parents who provide emotional and financial support for their adult children. But my ongoing caution is to first ask yourself whether your help truly helps them, or makes them feel dependent, or leads them to feel entitled rather than appreciative.

A recent post of mine, "Enough Already! Stop Trying to Prove You Were a Good Parent," is about parents internally feeling they need to continuously prove they are a good parent to their struggling adult child. In this post, I want to share what to say when you say no, and your adult child responds with manipulative, guilt-injecting responses that may make you cave in. By cave in, I mean changing your no to yes while inwardly knowing that you are just creating more unhealthy dependency. Please hear that, as parents, we face very complex dynamics of love, caring, anxiety, a desire to set boundaries, and a pull to take those boundaries based on what our adult children say to us.

Hopefully you agree that preparing specific responses in advance, rather than improvising in the moment, makes an enormous difference in how a backlash conversation goes. Below are four common reactions, along with a calm, firm, noncontrolling response to each, based on my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me! How to Stop Rescuing, Reduce Conflict, and Help Your Adult Child Move Forward.

How to Not Let These 4 Adult Child Comebacks Set You Back

  1. "You don’t love me.” Your 29-year-old son sends you a crisis-laden text about needing money for "an amazing investment opportunity." You explain that you have already provided them with money for their car repairs, and you hear back: "You say you love me, but obviously you don't because if you did, you would help me." Try saying back: “I love you completely. This isn’t about love. It’s about what I think will actually help you in both the short-term and long-term.”
  2. “You have the money, so why won’t you help?” You and your spouse are finally getting away, and you're on a lovely cruise. Your 32-year-old daughter texts you: "You and mom can go on that expensive cruise vacation while I can barely make ends meet working a crappy, soul-sucking job." Try saying back, “What is in our bank accounts and our comfort zones for providing money to you are not related. We are happy to have a calm, constructive conversation about other ways we can support you while you take steps to improve your job situation."
  3. "Don’t expect to see me for a while.” Ah, talk about a gut punch from your adult child! This line sends many parents into a tailspin. Try saying back: “I’ll miss you, and I understand you need some space. I still love you, and my answer hasn’t changed.”
  4. “Everyone else’s parents help them out.” Yep, that good ole, shaming-by-comparing-you-to-others maneuver can really knock you off balance if you let it. Try saying back: "I can’t speak for other families. I’m making this decision based on what I think is right for ours.”

The Takeaway

Notice what each response has in common: It doesn’t argue the underlying point at length, it doesn’t escalate, and it doesn’t reverse the decision. It simply restates your love and restates the boundary, calmly, and as many times as the conversation requires.

item.title: Consistent Exercise Builds Better Mood, Deeper Sleep
item.description:
Habit Formation

Consistent Exercise Builds Better Mood, Deeper Sleep

Two recent studies link a consistent exercise habit to better mood and rest.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • A study found that people who trained more consistently tended to report fewer depressive symptoms.
  • The best exercise for a person's mental health may simply be the one they will actually keep doing.
  • Exercise seems to help mood through one set of pathways and improve sleep through another.
Source: Kuiyibo Campos / Pexels

If you have ever wondered whether dragging yourself to the gym actually does anything for your mind or your sleep, two studies published within weeks of each other this summer offer an encouraging, and refreshingly practical, answer. Taken together, they suggest that building a consistent exercise habit may pay you two separate dividends: a steadier mood and more restful sleep. And, intriguingly, the mood benefit does not appear to simply be a side effect of sleeping better. They seem to be two distinct gifts from the same habit.

Two studies, one bigger picture

The first study, published July 22, 2026, in the Journal of Clinical Medicine, followed 349 people, mostly young adults, and examined how their physical activity related to both depressive symptoms and sleep quality (Hryniewicz et al., 2026). The researchers measured mood with the Beck Depression Inventory and sleep with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, then used a statistical technique to tease apart what was driving what.

The second study, published September 1, 2026, in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise analyzed data from 702,007 Japanese adults who completed annual health checkups in two consecutive years (Miyagi et al., 2026). This let the researchers see what happened to people's sleep when they started exercising, kept it up, or stopped.

A quick aside: the lead author of that second study shares a surname with cinema's most famous sensei. There is no relation, of course, but the coincidence is too fitting to ignore, because the training philosophy of "Karate Kid"'s fictional Mr. Miyagi maps almost eerily onto what this very real Miyagi and colleagues found. "Wax on, wax off" was about quiet, repeated practice producing benefits the student cannot feel accumulating until, one day, they have. That is precisely the shape of the science here: No dramatic single workout changes you, but consistent exercise builds something that eventually becomes undeniable. It is a serendipitous echo of the films.

The studies took place in different countries, with different age groups, and with very different sizes, yet the two arrive at complementary conclusions.

Consistency and intensity matter more than the type of workout

Source: Ivan S ./ Pexels

One of the most freeing findings from the smaller study is that the kind of exercise did not seem to matter much. Running, lifting, cycling, team sports—no single type stood out as superior for mood or sleep. What did stand out was intensity and volume. People who trained harder and more consistently tended to report fewer depressive symptoms (Hryniewicz et al., 2026).

Experience mattered. Participants who had been training for three to five years reported lower depression scores than those with less than a year under their belt. This hints that benefits may accumulate over time, that exercise is less a quick fix and more a long game.

Stop agonizing over whether you've chosen the "right" workout. The best exercise for your mental health may simply be the one you will actually keep doing.

Building the habit improves how rested you feel

Among more than 700,000 adults, those who started a regular exercise habit were significantly more likely to report improved sleep restfulness the following year, and those who maintained their habit continued to feel the benefit, even people who were already exercising but still felt unrested (Miyagi et al., 2026). Those who quit exercising tended to lose ground.

It was structured, regular exercise, not merely general daily "physical activity" like incidental walking, that showed the most consistent link to better sleep restfulness. Deliberately building an exercise routine appeared more reliably tied to feeling rested than just being generally busy on your feet.

Mood and sleep may be separate wins

Here is the finding most likely to reshape how we think about this. It would be easy to assume that exercise lifts your mood mainly by helping you sleep better. But the July study largely did not support that idea. When the researchers looked closely, sleep quality did not appear to be the bridge between exercise and reduced depressive symptoms (Hryniewicz et al., 2026).

Put the two studies side by side and a compelling picture emerges: exercise seems to help your mood through one set of pathways and improve your sleep through another. You are not trading one benefit for the other. You may be earning both, independently, from the same effort.

What this means for you

If you have been waiting for a reason to start moving, or to recommit, here is an evidence-based nudge:

  • Pick something you will repeat. The type of exercise mattered far less than sticking with it. Choose what fits your life.
  • Effort counts. More intense, higher-volume training was tied to better mood outcomes. Within safe limits, don't be afraid to push a little.
  • Think in years, not days. The mood benefits appeared strongest in people with a longer training history. Consistency compounds.
  • Starting helps, quitting hurts. Beginning and maintaining exercise was linked to feeling more rested, while stopping reversed gains.
  • Two benefits for one habit. You may improve both your mood and your sleep, and you don't have to sleep better first to feel better emotionally.

A word of caution

Source: Ferhat Kocakaya / Pexels

Both studies are observational, meaning they show strong associations, not ironclad proof that exercise causes these improvements.

The mood study was also cross-sectional—a single snapshot in time—and relied partly on self-reported activity.

People who feel better may also be more inclined to exercise, so the arrow can point both ways.

Still, these findings align with a large existing body of research and land on the same encouraging message: moving your body, consistently and with some effort, is one of the most accessible tools you have for protecting both your mind and your rest.

item.title: 3 Lessons for Life, Well Lived
item.description:
Decision-Making

3 Lessons for Life, Well Lived

To live well, test assumptions, create more options, and stay intentional.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Intentional living begins by questioning assumptions before accepting them as hard facts.
  • When our attention narrows, creating more options can reveal new paths we had failed to consider.
  • Consider not only what a choice gives you now but which new possibilities it opens or closes for your future.

I start every business ethics class with students repeating the same thing, which I call my three lessons for life, well lived:

  1. Don’t take anything for granted.
  2. You always have more options than you think.
  3. To get the most out of something, be as intentional as possible.

The constant repetition is my way of trying to make it stick, both as a business and an ethics mantra. Whether they end up in corporate America, the nonprofit space, or doing something else, I want them to take an entrepreneurial approach to life, where they pursue opportunities that speak to what they care about and that add value to their life and the world around them. The mantra also allows them to live ethically in the way I understand ethics, which is not simply knowing how to talk about moral problems but also knowing how to approach those problems with greater agency and deliberateness.

Don’t take anything for granted.

When people first hear this lesson, they quickly take it to be about gratitude—that we should appreciate what we have. This is good advice, since if we take our life for granted, we may end up living on autopilot, allowing other people and circumstances to determine our direction. Yet, this is not what I mean. I mean that we should not confuse the way something has been presented with the way it actually is or must be.

Be wary of conclusions disguised as facts. There are times when genuine constraints exist. At other times, a “seeming” constraint is only a person’s interpretation or a failure of imagination to see another way.

For example, I once spoke with someone trying to move into a new industry. After several conversations, potential employers would tell him that he was very talented but that they could not see where he would fit. He treated those comments as final judgments and politely walked away. I encouraged him to hear them more carefully. They were not necessarily saying he had nothing to contribute. They were saying that they did not have a ready-made role for him. They may also not be willing to take a chance on someone who isn’t an easy fit. However, even if a company may not have an existing position for you, it may still have a problem you can help solve. You may be able to show them how you could fit in a way that recognizes their risk aversion. This will not work 100 percent of the time, but creating an option for yourself is better than accepting that there are no options available.

This leads to the second lesson.

You always have more options than you think.

Instead of choosing to walk away or plead for a job that does not exist, he could propose something different: a short-term project, a trial engagement, or an opportunity to address a specific need. The goal is not to pressure someone into giving you what you want but to find a way for mutual benefit that people don’t currently see.

Turning zero-sum situations into positive-sum situations doesn’t only work in business; you can take the same approach in your personal life as well.

When focusing on results or when the stakes are high, our field of vision tends to narrow. If we don’t get the one thing we’re shooting for, we think we will end up with nothing. In the same way, ethical challenges can become “dilemmas,” where we only see two bad options to choose from. However, when we think about what we are trying to do, rather than what we are trying to attain, we may start looking for other ways to do what we want. Generating more than two alternatives can help us understand which costs are truly unavoidable and which exist only because we accept someone else’s framing.

Being creative to get more of what you want in the moment, however, is not enough. You also need to set yourself up so that you can have more options in the future. This means taking a long view about choices, thinking not only about what they get you now but also what they open up or close off in the future.

That is where the third lesson comes in.

To get the most out of something, be as intentional as possible.

To “get the most” out of life, “most” shouldn’t be understood in terms of quantity but rather quality. It’s not simply about climbing that ladder but about making sure that the ladder is leaning against the right wall. To use another metaphor, when thinking about the life roads you embark on, take the turns that keep you going in the direction that you want to go and not just the ones that are the easiest—or most common—to take.

This means trying to learn and grow through each experience. Think not only about the external benefits a choice gives you, such as money, prestige, and acclaim, but also the internal benefits you can develop, such as the skills and tools you can acquire to do whatever you choose to do next.

You can’t always guarantee that a decision will work out, but you can be sure that every opportunity is a learning opportunity.

Living intentionally also means developing habits and structuring your environment so that routine choices don't consume the attention and energy you need to carry out larger commitments. It means establishing practices that help you move forward, while remaining attentive enough to notice when your direction needs to change.

A cord of three strands is not easily broken.

Taken together, these three lessons can move you from being a passive participant in life to taking a more active role in shaping it. They may not give you the results you want, but they do help ensure that the life you choose to live and the person you choose to become are genuinely your own.

item.title: Is Laughing at Yourself Good for Your Mental Health?
item.description:
Laughter

Is Laughing at Yourself Good for Your Mental Health?

Empirical findings on the importance of taking yourself less seriously.

Posted September 3, 2026

Is laughing at yourself good for you? Is this something we should feel encouraged to do? Is it good for our mental health? The findings are somewhat ambiguous, but they also highlight the importance of not taking ourselves too seriously.

Some of us laugh at ourselves. Some others would never do such a thing. Which one is the better coping mechanism? Oddly, in terms of the history of thinking about our own mind, the option of laughing at ourselves was not always taken to be a real option. In fact, the Greek philosopher Plato argued that not only is it unwise to laugh at ourselves, it is actually impossible to do so, as laughter is something that is only appropriate towards people who are in some sense below us (and we can't be, by definition, below ourselves).

Plato aside, some people clearly do routinely laugh at themselves, a phenomenon that has been studied experimentally in the last couple of decades. More generally, people differ quite radically in terms of their humor style. And one specific style that has been studied extensively is what is often called "self-defeating" or "self-deprecating" humor. And the question often asked in these studies is whether people who go in for this style of humor are better or worse off in terms of life satisfaction, happiness, and mental health.

Interestingly, the results are somewhat inconclusive. Some suggest that this form of humor is, in fact, bad for you. It seems to be correlated with anxiety and even suicidal ideation. Other studies found that laughing at yourself is actually good for your well-being and affective resilience as well as self-esteem and mental health. In a famous study, people were presented with their own reflection in funhouse-style distorting mirrors. Those who were capable of genuinely laughing at their own reflection seemed to have exhibited fewer negative emotions. How can we make sense of these conflicting findings?

One thing to notice is that many of these studies found correlational evidence. Some subjects may have used laughing at themselves as a coping strategy, but it is whatever problems they were coping with that were primarily correlated with the negative mental health results and not the coping strategy.

But an even more important ambiguity here is that laughing at yourself is really a combination of two things. First, actively using humor as a defense or coping mechanism. And this is the aspect that these studies focused on. However, another aspect of laughing at yourself that needs to be teased apart from humor is taking yourself less seriously. And many of the experiments that found a positive correlation between laughing at yourself and well-being (like the funhouse mirror experiment) are actually about taking yourself less seriously and not about what kind of jokes you make.

More generally, self-deprecating humor can be used in a variety of ways. It can be a part of your very rigid self-image: I am the kind of guy who makes self-deprecating jokes—like Chandler in the sitcom Friends. But such rigid self-image often goes straight against taking yourself less seriously. What really drives the positive effects of laughing at yourself is, in fact, the much more widespread phenomenon of not taking yourself too seriously.

item.title: What Does 'ADHD Is Real' Even Mean?
item.description:
ADHD

What Does 'ADHD Is Real' Even Mean?

“ADHD is real” conflates real difficulties, an institutional category, and biology.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Brain scans only show group averages, not a neurological marker that identifies an individual with ADHD.
  • High heritability does not show that ADHD—or any individual’s difficulties—is largely caused by genes.
  • Recognition and support do not require making diagnosis the explanation for people’s struggles.

Following the Channel 4 documentary The Great ADHD Myth?, which aired in August this year, the Royal College of Psychiatrists issued a statement about it in which it described attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) as a “well-established neurodevelopmental disorder,” the legitimacy of which "should not be questioned." An accompanying statement went further, stating, "Whatever you think about ADHD, its scientific basis is not in doubt."

These responses, and others, cite evidence of genetic and neurological differences, responses to stimulants, and institutional consensus as establishing the diagnosis of ADHD as “real” and beyond scientific doubt, treated as though they establish it as a distinct neurobiological entity, substantially genetic in origin. These are scientific claims that very much depend on evidence. The crucial question, then, is what the cited evidence actually establishes.

In a recent BMJ response that I co-authored with Joanna Moncrieff, Lucy Johnstone, and James Davies, we distinguished among the “experiential reality,” “institutional reality,” and “ontological reality” of "ADHD is real." These are very different claims, and they are used interchangeably in a way that misleads.

Three meanings of “ADHD is real”

First, "ADHD is real" is used to refer to the reality of the experiences and behaviours that are diagnosed as ADHD—difficulty with concentration, organisation, impulsivity, restlessness, and the demands of everyday life, sometimes in the extreme. This is ADHD's experiential reality. These experiences and behaviours are undoubtedly real.

The second meaning refers to the institutional reality of ADHD. It is a recognised psychiatric diagnosis, used by clinicians and healthcare systems and increasingly taken up by people as a way of understanding themselves. It is a diagnosis with material consequences and services organised around it, and, again, there is no doubt of its reality in this sense.

The third meaning of "ADHD is real" is that the diagnosis of ADHD has an ontological reality—that it identifies a discrete underlying neurodevelopmental disorder that explains the behaviours and experiences by which it is diagnosed. Much of the debate turns on this meaning. Unlike the first two meanings, this is not simply a factual claim but a scientific and conceptual hypothesis—one that remains thoroughly open to dispute, as I will show below.

Much confusion, polarisation—and, it must be said, misinformation—results from conflating these meanings. As we say in our BMJ response, it arises:

"From moving between these claims uncritically, particularly by conflating the first and third: the reality of the experiences and behaviours is treated as evidence that the diagnostic category and attached neurodevelopmental explanation are also real and true. This rhetorical move often curtails debate about the nature and causes of the problems we currently refer to as ADHD."

So, let's look at what the evidence actually shows us in relation to this third claim. I will focus here only on the two most important sources of evidence.

Where is the neurological disorder?

We often see claims that neuroimaging studies show that the brains of people diagnosed with ADHD are different. Neuroimaging studies, however, only identify (small) average differences between groups, while the relevant distributions substantially overlap, findings vary across studies, and many reported associations are shared with other diagnostic categories. In other words, they produce no single, consistent neurological finding in individuals diagnosed with ADHD, which can be illustrated with two examples. First, such group-level differences may be entirely absent in someone diagnosed with ADHD, yet present in someone who does not have the diagnosis. Second, the same differences may also be found in people given entirely different psychiatric diagnoses. We can see, then, that the findings themselves do not tell us anything specific about an "ADHD brain" or pattern of neurological functioning specific to people diagnosed with ADHD. It should be clear, therefore, that it is very misleading to suggest that these findings establish the neurodevelopmental status of the ADHD diagnosis.

Heritability is not genetic causation

Genetic evidence is often used in much the same way. ADHD is frequently described as “highly heritable,” and this is commonly presented—and understood—as evidence that the experiences and behaviours grouped underneath the diagnosis are largely caused by genes. But that is not what a heritability estimate means, and heritability findings cannot establish such a claim. Heritability estimates how much of the variation in a measured trait, within a particular population and under particular environmental conditions, is attributed to differences between individuals that are considered heritable. It neither tells us how much of an individual’s difficulties are caused by genes nor that there is any specific genetic mechanism. Furthermore, heritability can also change as environments change and does not, by itself, distinguish genetic effects from the developmental processes through which genes and environments interact. So, again, it should be clear that suggesting or implying that "ADHD is largely genetic" is very misleading.

Diagnosis is not the alternative to neglect

Neither set of findings, then, establishes a discrete neurodevelopmental entity or specific causal mechanism. So, the third sense of "ADHD is real" is not substantiated. Description becomes explanation, while group-level associations become claims about what individuals "have." And this is where the problem arises. Rightful criticism of the ontological reality of ADHD is repeatedly presented as though it were equivalent to saying that people’s difficulties are imaginary or that they should be denied help, which is to conflate the first and third meanings outlined above. This is done by psychiatric professionals and institutions, which is deeply problematic, as people look to these institutions as authoritative sources of knowledge about what it means—and what it says—about them.

As we conclude our BMJ response:

“The public are being misinformed by psychiatric institutions and other organisations in claiming that the science is settled. The public deserves to know the real status of the scientific research and have access to alternative ideas and approaches to the problems conceptualised as ADHD."

As Nobel Prize-winning physicist Richard Feynman famously put it, “Science is the belief in the ignorance of experts."

Critiquing the diagnosis of ADHD is not suggesting that the experiences, behaviours, and impairments grouped under ADHD are unreal, trivial, or undeserving of support. It concerns the psychiatric explanation of these in terms of an underlying neurodevelopmental disorder, something that is not established by the evidence. Recognition and support do not depend on accepting a psychiatric explanation; both can be provided on the basis of assessed need. To insist that the status of ADHD is "beyond scientific doubt" is not only obviously unscientific but also serves to close down precisely the unanswered questions at the root of the issues we are seeing.

item.title: With AI, Has Your Mirror Started to Agree?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

With AI, Has Your Mirror Started to Agree?

How AI amplifies what we believe about ourselves, others, and the world.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Whereas internet search gives us results, generative AI outputs deliver us interpretation.
  • AI’s capacity for ultra-customized answers tends to reinforce our existing beliefs.
  • Deliberately designed, evidence-based conversations with AI can reduce belief in conspiracy theories.
Once upon a time our environment had the inconvenient habit of talking back. This is changing with AI.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

For most of human history, reality has had the inconvenient habit of talking back.

Other people disagree with us. Facts refuse to fit. A colleague questions our interpretation. A friend says we may have been unfair. A doctor gives us an answer we did not want. The newspaper contains something that irritates us. Somewhere between our convictions and the world, there has usually been friction.

Artificial intelligence is changing the flavor of friction

Increasingly, we turn to artificial intelligence (AI) after an argument, during uncertainty, when trying to understand an illness, interpreting someone else’s behaviour or making sense of events. We arrive carrying a hypothesis: I think my boss is undermining me. I suspect this treatment is dangerous. I feel my partner is manipulating me. I have always believed that… Our remarks may be spoken innocently, yet they are anchoring the Chatbot in the orientation that we expect its answer to be.

The machine listens. And more often than not, it agrees with us. This has consequences on our (in)ability to learn from online conversations. Yet the emerging risk is much bigger than misinformation. AI is bound to become a belief amplifier: an endlessly available conversational partner capable of converting a hunch into an explanation, an explanation into a narrative, and a narrative into something that begins to resemble reality. As the bot uses every element that it has available on us from past and present chats, it is equipped to build a storyline that is personalized to be believed.

From confirmation bias to confirmation machinery

Confirmation bias is ancient. Humans tend to seek, notice, and remember information that supports what they already believe. AI gives that tendency an extraordinarily responsive new environment.

A 2025 study spanning 21 studies across subjects including health, finance, politics, and society found what researchers called the “narrow search effect.” Our existing beliefs influence the questions we ask; search systems then return highly relevant answers to those questions. The combination can leave people with information environments that increasingly resemble their starting assumptions. The effect appeared across Google, ChatGPT, and AI-enabled Bing.

This is preoccupying because conversational AI goes considerably further than conventional search. Whereas internet search gives us results, generative AI outputs deliver us interpretation. They connect fragments, supply motives, construct causal chains, and produce eloquent explanations around the premise embedded in our questions. A suspicion may therefore return dressed in paragraphs, examples, and apparent logic.

The hybrid loop is simple: I believe → I prompt → AI personalizes → I feel confirmed → I prompt more narrowly → AI confirms more precisely → My beliefs are confirmed.

Each turn can make the next one easier to believe.

What started as “I think” becomes “I know,” which turns smoothly into “I am sure”

The consequences become especially interesting when the topic touches our ego and self-esteem.

A 2026 study examined sycophancy—the tendency of AI systems to excessively agree with or validate their users. Across 11 leading models, researchers found that AI affirmed users’ behavior 49 percent more often than humans did, including situations involving deception, illegality, and other harmful conduct. Furthermore, the study found that after interacting with sycophantic AI, people became more convinced that they were right in interpersonal conflicts and less willing to take responsibility or repair relationships. Remarkably, participants also preferred the more sycophantic systems and trusted them more than bots that were pushing back.

Are we keen to be trapped?

Being understood feels good. Being validated feels even better. Sadly, neither feeling tells us whether our interpretation is accurate.

The same dynamic that impacts the beliefs that we have about ourselves affects what we believe about the world. Suppose someone begins convinced that immigration causes rising crime, that nuclear power is inherently unsafe, that a particular food cures disease, or that an economic policy inevitably produces inflation.

The first prompt will seldom say: “Please provide the most balanced possible assessment of this proposition.” It may say: "Why is nuclear energy so dangerous?" Or "Explain how immigration is increasing crime." The wording contains a worldview. An AI answering the question literally can furnish the evidence, arguments, and vocabulary needed to strengthen it. Research on health information has identified this danger. AI’s capacity for ultra-customized answers tends to reinforce existing health beliefs, obscure medical consensus, and magnify misinformation.

Scale changes the significance of the problem

Once AI can produce polished arguments for millions of personalized premises, fringe interpretations no longer need a newspaper, institution, or large community to give them intellectual form. Every person can have a private editorial department constructing an increasingly convincing version of their preferred reality. This is how amplification can lead toward mainstreaming. Ideas acquire fluency. Fluency gives them familiarity. Familiarity can begin to feel like plausibility.

There is encouraging evidence here, too.

Researchers have found that deliberately designed, evidence-based conversations with AI can reduce belief in conspiracy theories. In a preregistered 2025 study, personalized conversations significantly reduced participants’ confidence in conspiracy and other epistemically unwarranted beliefs. The effect came from the quality and relevance of the arguments themselves—no matter whether participants believed they were speaking to an AI or a human interlocutor. Ultimately, the problem is only partially the technology we are interacting with. More importantly, we need to build a mindset marked by curiosity, and build curiosity, combined with the capability to not only listen but also hear others.

LISTEN before you believe

A simple practice can help. When a conversation with AI touches something you care deeply about, LISTEN.

L — Locate your starting belief. Before asking AI, finish the sentence: “I currently think…” Making your prior assumption visible prevents it from disappearing inside the prompt.

I — Invite interruption. Ask AI: “What am I overlooking?” “Which evidence would weaken my conclusion?” Give the machine explicit permission to disturb the story.

S — Separate support from substance. Notice when AI is validating an emotion and when it is validating a factual claim. “That sounds painful” and “Your interpretation is correct” perform very different functions.

T — Triangulate. For consequential questions, move beyond one conversation. Check primary evidence, credible independent sources, and, where appropriate, another human being. One beautifully coherent answer remains one answer.

E — Expose the frame. Ask the question again from another angle. Remove emotionally loaded assumptions. Reverse the perspective. Ask AI how different framings change its conclusion.

N — Notice what changed. At the end, ask yourself: What did I learn? What evidence changed my mind?

Listening in the hybrid age requires space for critical thinking.
